title: OPINION: Investigate the U.S. Envoy to Syria and Iraq
content:
By David L. Phillips*

OXFORD, UK | 20 November 2026 (IDN) — Tom Barrack’s handling of U.S. policy towards Syria deserves congressional scrutiny. So do reports that he advocated a role for a business associate’s firm in a major regional oil pipeline project. The House Foreign Affairs Committee should examine whether his diplomatic responsibilities and private business relationships were adequately separated.

An investigation should establish the facts without assuming its conclusion. Questions about impartiality deserve examination even where personal financial gain has not been demonstrated.

Reuters reported in October that Barrack promoted TI Capital, founded by his business partner Ziad Ghandour, for the Kirkuk–Baniyas pipeline project. Barrack disclosed a stake in ACD-TI Oakley Investment LLC, a separate property venture managed by TI Capital. Reuters found no evidence that he would profit from the pipeline. The State Department denied that he had a financial interest or role in the project and said he complied with ethics rules. (www.jpost.com

title: 2026 Water Conference: What’s at stake for Asia and the Pacific?
content:
By Lorenzo Santucci, Anshuman Varma, and Michael Koch*

BANGKOK, Thailand | 20 November 2026 (IDN) — As the global community gathers in Abu Dhabi for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference (December 8-10) to review progress and accelerate action towards SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation), the stakes for Asia and the Pacific are particularly high.

Despite important advances in recent decades, progress towards Goal 6 remains uneven and too slow to meet the 2030 targets. Climate change is adding further complexities through intensifying droughts, floods and water-related disasters across the region. In May, ministers, policymakers and stakeholders from across the region highlighted both the scale of the challenges and the opportunities to accelerate action. A clear message emerged: while the region remains off track on several SDG 6 targets, the region is home to innovative solutions and strong leadership that can help drive progress.

title: ESSAY: Beyond the Hive — Freedom, Community, and the Rivals of Amziah King
content:
By Sam Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 18 November 2026 (IDN) — Andrew Patterson’s The Rivals of Amziah King (2026) appears at first to be a story about competition, community, and revenge. But beneath its exuberant musical performances, eccentric characters, and increasingly violent confrontations lies a more radical philosophical proposition: that human beings are capable of organizing their lives according to principles fundamentally different from those governing capitalist exchange. The film’s recurring images of honeybee colonies are crucial to this vision, as are its extraordinary scenes of communal music-making. Together, they suggest a conception of freedom that is neither individualistic nor hierarchical, but realized through relationships of mutual dependence, responsiveness, and care.

title: OPINION: Time to Suffocate the New Nuclear Arms Race
content:
In Shenzhen, three presidents need a common nuclear language. No treaty is on offer when Xi, Putin and Trump meet on Thursday. A statement of basic principles, and a mandate for talks among the five nuclear-weapon States, would be achievement enough.

By Tariq Rauf*

VIENNA | 17 November 2026 (IDN) — On 19 November, on the margins of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump are due to sit down together for the first time.1 Between them they command roughly nine of every ten nuclear warheads on earth.2 US officials already are playing the meeting down as an “entry point” from which no agreement is expected.3 They are right about the agreement, and wrong if they think that makes the meeting inconsequential. The most useful thing the three leaders can do in Shenzhen is not to haggle over numbers but to agree on “basic principles” governing strategic relations between them and nuclear weapons.

title: OPINION: African Democracy on Life Support
content:
By The Rev. Gabriel Odima*

MINNESOTA, USA | 16 November 2026 (IDN) — Africa has become a household name across North America, Europe, Australia, South America and Asia. The only images beaming on the world’s television screens are hunger-stricken skeletons, civil wars, political abductions, human rights abuses and a move towards single-party or no-party rule in countries like Uganda, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Niger, Benin, Tanzania, Gabon and Sudan, to name a few. Democracy is on life support across Africa, and this is a troubling trend.

In the case of Uganda, the military regime, from its installation in 1986 by the gun and bloodshed, has consistently, arrogantly and cynically suppressed and never permitted citizens and their organised political parties to enjoy the freedom to hold opinions on political or public matters, except the opinions of the regime.

In August 1992, the military rulers in Uganda decided to discard their cloak of disguise, which had enabled them since 1986 to falsely present their regime as a coalition in which political parties were represented.

title: EEPA reports on South Sudan elections postponed to February 2027
content:
BRUSSELS | 16 November 2026 (IDN | EEPA) — The following are the situation reports on the situation in Ethiopia, the situation in Sudan, the regional and international situation, South Sudan elections postponed to February 2027, Sudan to fight gold trafficking, ongoing clashes around Badme

  • Escalating clashes around Badme, the disputed border town between Ethiopia and Eritrea, have been ongoing for over six days, involving Ethiopian drone strikes and heavy Eritrean artillery. 
  • Ethiopian National Defence Forces’ (ENDF) troops are now present in Gemhalo, located between Sheraro and Badme, while the Eritrean Defence Forces are reportedly stationed near Badme. 
  • Badme itself remains outside the control of any military force. Eritrean intelligence personnel have been seen in the town. 
  • Families have been displaced amid ongoing clashes in Badme, with residents stating that shops and markets have been closed. 
  • Public protests erupted in Jimma city, southwestern Oromia, sparked by the fatal shooting of a former ENDF soldier and fueled by mounting anger over forced conscription, security, extortion, and uncompensated urban evictions.

title: Kazakhstan and Japan Renew Test-Ban Appeal as Treaty Deadlock Persists
content:
Thirty years after opening for signature, the CTBT has broad international support but still lacks nine ratifications required for entry into force

By Ramesh Jaura

BERLIN | 15 November 2026 (IDN) — Kazakhstan and Japan have renewed calls for an end to nuclear testing as the treaty intended to prohibit all nuclear explosions remains blocked, three decades after it opened for signature.

Their appeal, made at a September commemoration at the United Nations Office at Nairobi, comes as preparations for enforcing the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) continue despite the political impasse. An inspection exercise in Namibia is testing capabilities that cannot be used under the treaty until it enters into force.

The contrast exposes a central weakness in the international effort to prevent renewed testing: governments have built a global detection network, but have yet to activate the agreement that would authorise inspectors to investigate a suspected violation on the ground.

title: Sudan’s Empty Warehouses Leave Millions Without Shelter
content:
As relief stocks run out, expanding drone warfare, foreign arms supplies and divided diplomacy are worsening one of the world’s largest humanitarian emergencies

By Ramesh Jaura

BERLIN | 12 November 2026 (IDN) – Winter nights in Darfur and northern Sudan can be bitterly cold. Many families displaced by war are nevertheless sleeping beneath plastic sheets, in crowded public buildings or beside damaged houses.

Some have returned to their towns only to find that their homes have been destroyed or looted, water and electricity are unavailable and the nearest clinic is closed.

The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, and the International Organization for Migration, IOM, warned on 6 November that their stocks of tents, blankets and other essentials were almost exhausted. An estimated 15.4 million people need emergency shelter or basic household items, but available funds allow relief agencies to give priority to only about one in ten.

Even that reduced target has not been met. Only 936,000 people have received assistance.

Mohamed Refaat, head of IOM’s mission in Sudan, said the agency’s warehouses were empty. A convoy of 16 trucks that reached Darfur carried the last of its available stocks.
